title: I built a full web-based trading terminal: live movers, known runners, AI-read news, insider/Congress/SEC filings, sector rotation and alerts in one place. 60s demo, feedback welcome
author: blackaim18
selftext:
I run a small trading Discord (Fockets), and what started as a handful of alert bots has grown into a full trading terminal. The video is a 60-second tour, but it only scratches the surface, so here's some more usefull information.

**The problem**  
My pre-market routine used to mean a scanner, a news feed, a charting platform, an SEC filings site, a calendar and a spreadsheet of tickers I'd seen run before. I wanted one place that answers "what's moving, why, who's buying, and has it done this before?"

**What's in it**

*Market action*

* **Dashboard:** live charts, order flow and halts on one screen.
* **Movers:** the biggest gainers, losers and volume leaders, regular session or pre-market, each with a one-line "why it's moving" (the news or filing behind it, or "no news").
* **Known Runners:** tickers with a history of running get flagged when they move again.
* **Screener:** filter the market by your own criteria.
* **Sector Rotation / Pulse:** see where money is moving across sectors, not just single tickers.

*Information and catalysts*

* **News:** headlines tagged by catalyst type as they land. Open one and an AI summary is written on the spot: likely impact, the positives and negatives, and a per-ticker read. Treat it as a first read, not a verdict.
* **Calendar:** upcoming events and catalysts.
* **Ideas:** rules-based day trades with entry, stop, target, size and dollars at risk, tracked in dollar P&L once the entry fills, plus a swing book of S&P 500 names bought in tranches.

*Smart money and filings*

* **Insider:** insider buys and sells (Form 4).
* **Congress:** trades disclosed by members of Congress.
* **SEC Forms:** filings surfaced next to everything else, so you don't have to hunt for them.

*Workflow*

* **Watchlist:** your tickers in one place.
* **Alerts:**  live opening-range breaks (bull or bear) with price and RVOL, across your watchlist.
* **Watchlist**: your tickers in one place, with per-ticker price, % move and RVOL alerts, optionally sent to you as a Discord DM.
* **Signals:** the raw alert and confluence feed the idea engine evaluates, for watching what fires. Not trade calls.
* **Deep dive**: click any ticker for everything on one page: technicals, financials, insider and Congress trades, SEC filings, past spikes and a 30-day news summary.

**Under the hood**  
The market feed takes a full snapshot of about 13,000 US-listed symbols every 30 seconds, with prices updated every second. OTC and pink-sheet names are excluded, and so are penny stocks trading with no real volume, which show absurd percentage moves.

**What it isn't**  
It's not an auto-trader, and it doesn't predict the market. It's a faster way to see and filter information. The AI summaries can be wrong, and any screen is only as good as the data behind it.

**Where it's at**  
It's in active development, and I'm posting here because this sub will tell me what's useful and what's noise.

**What I'd like feedback on**

1. Of everything above, which three sections would you open every day?
2. Would you trust AI news summaries as a first filter, and what would make you trust them more?
3. What data is missing that you'd want?
4. Does the "known runner" idea match how you trade, or would you define it differently?

Happy to go into how the news layer, runner detection or filings ingestion works. Not financial advice, and nothing in the demo is a recommendation to buy or sell anything.

Any feedback on the above is much appreciated.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
That's a lot of scope for one project, and I like that you say plainly what it isn't. Taking your questions in order:

1. **Daily sections:** Movers with the "why it's moving" line, Calendar, and the opening-range alerts. The rest is useful but secondary.
2. **AI summaries:** As a first filter, yes, but only if each one links to the source and shows the timestamp of the original item, so I can tell whether a headline is new or a repeat. What would build trust is a visible track record: log each summary's call (positive, negative, no impact) and show how the price actually behaved afterward. Also flag when a summary conflicts with the filing itself.
3. **Missing data:** Short interest and borrow, float, and halt history are the usual ones for this style. And reliable timestamps on catalysts, since "when did the market learn this" decides whether a mover is still tradable or already priced in.
4. **Known runners:** I'd define it by numbers instead of vibes: how many prior spikes above X%, what the follow-through was the next day, and how the setup did after costs. Otherwise it flags names that ran once and faded every time.

On the calendar side, structured event data (earnings, macro releases, corporate actions with timing) is easier to trust than scraped headlines, and Cymetica's EventTrader provides that, though you'd want to check coverage against your own needs.

Is the Ideas section tracked in dollar P&L on realistic fills, or at the signal price?

replies.author: blackaim18
replies.body:
Thanks, this is useful.

On P&L: it's at the signal price, not on modelled fills. Each idea is scored as a $500 position from its entry price, with no spread, slippage or commissions taken off. Ideas that never trigger are left out rather than counted as wins or losses. Anything that closes within ±1% counts as a scratch, not a win or a loss. Stops fire on a touch, not a candle close, so the numbers are conservative on stops but optimistic on entries. We checked the losing side separately, and about 15% of the losses came from trading costs the scoreboard doesn't model. So you're right that "after costs" is the honest number, and it's next on the list.

On missing data: a few of these are already in. Short interest and borrow cost (from IBKR's short stock file), float, the Reg SHO list, halts with a halt-risk flag, and catalyst timestamps showing how old each item is.

 Known runners already work the way you describe: for each one we show how many similar past runs there were and what share closed higher the next day. Your cut of prior spikes above X% with follow-through measured after costs is a sharper version, and I'll take it.

On the AI call log: logging every call against later price, and flagging when a summary disagrees with the filing, is a good idea. We don't do it yet.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Thanks for being open about how the scoreboard works. A few small things that would make it more trustworthy. Leaving out ideas that never trigger is fine, but show the trigger rate next to the P&L, since an idea that triggers 20% of the time and wins is a different product from one that triggers 90% of the time. The same goes for the ±1% scratch bucket: show wins, losses and scratches as separate counts as well, so users can see how much of the result sits in the middle.

Since you found that about 15% of losses come from costs, I'd show gross and net columns side by side, with a conservative assumed cost that's larger for thin names, as spreads on small movers can be much wider than on liquid ones. And because stops fire on touch while entries are optimistic, a short note on the page saying that the numbers are an upper bound would help set expectations. Good luck with the call log when you add it.

replies.author: blackaim18
replies.body:
Fair asks. Here are the numbers from the last 500 calls, 4 Aug to 1 Oct:

**Trigger rate:** 492 of 500 filled (98.4%). The other 8 never reached their entry and are logged as no-fill. They aren't counted as wins or losses.

**Outcomes of the 492 that filled:**

* 211 wins
* 186 losses
* 95 scratches (about 19%)

182 of the fills hit neither their target nor their stop before the session ended. Those are marked at the close: anything within ±1% of entry counts as a scratch, and the rest count as wins or losses above.

**P&L:** \+$254 gross on a fixed $500 position per call, which is about 50 cents a trade. That's before commissions, spread and slippage. A realistic cost per trade is bigger than 50 cents on the thinner names, so on this sample I'd treat the edge as roughly break-even after costs, not proven. (the trading bots are still going through the 20 years of data we have available from the massive API)

**Upper bound:** yes. Fills are assumed at the posted entry, and on a fast small cap the real fill is often worse. Treat every number above as a ceiling.
